abstracts.abstract: Mining contrast patterns from evolving data streams presents fundamental challenges due to the exponential search space and dynamic nature of underlying distributions. Traditional approaches rely on anti-monotonicity constraints that become ineffective when distributions shift over time. This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for contrast pattern mining in non-stationary environments, establishing formal connections between distribution dynamics and pattern stability measures. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the conventional frequency-based paradigm fails to capture meaningful discriminative patterns when temporal drift occurs, leading us to propose a new definition of contrast patterns based on temporal stability and divergence quantification. We derive theoretical conditions under which optimal contrast patterns can be identified in polynomial time, contradicting the conventional wisdom that such patterns require exponential search. The framework provides rigorous guarantees for pattern mining under distribution shift, enabling the development of algorithms that adapt to changing data characteristics without exhaustive enumeration. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world temporal datasets validate the theoretical findings, demonstrating that our approach identifies contrast patterns missed by existing methods. This work fundamentally reshapes the theoretical foundations of pattern mining in data streams, opening new research directions for knowledge discovery under temporal dynamics.

Feature selection remains a critical preprocessing step for high-dimensional classification tasks, yet theoretical understanding of why certain feature selection methods succeed or fail under specific conditions remains incomplete. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of stability in feature selection algorithms, establishing formal relationships between algorithmic stability, data distribution characteristics, and generalization performance. We extend classical uniform convergence theory to the feature selection domain, deriving tighter generalization bounds for methods based on feature interdependence modeling. Our analysis reveals that existing stability measures fail to capture the full picture of algorithmic behavior, leading us to propose a refined notion of pairwise feature stability that more accurately predicts downstream classification performance. The theoretical framework provides precise conditions under which different feature selection strategies achieve optimal results, enabling principled guidance for method selection in practical applications. We demonstrate that our improved bounds lead to a new feature selection algorithm with theoretical guarantees exceeding those of state-of-the-art methods. Extensive experiments on high-dimensional classification benchmarks validate the theoretical predictions, showing consistent improvements in both feature selection stability and classification accuracy. This work significantly advances our theoretical understanding of feature selection mechanisms, providing a principled foundation for improved machine learning pipelines.

Knowledge discovery from heterogeneous data sources spanning spatial, temporal, and network dimensions requires integrated systems capable of capturing complex cross-dimensional relationships. Existing distributed data mining frameworks treat different data modalities in isolation, missing crucial interdependencies that limit discovery quality. This paper presents GeoGraphStream, a novel distributed system architecture designed for unified knowledge discovery across heterogeneous data environments. The system introduces a unified representation model that encodes spatial proximity, temporal dynamics, and graph structure within a single computational framework, enabling pattern mining operations that span multiple data dimensions simultaneously. Our architecture employs a hierarchical message-passing mechanism that reduces communication overhead while maintaining global consistency across distributed nodes. The system implements novel operators for cross-dimensional pattern mining, including spatial-temporal graph motifs and geo-aware network clustering, which have no counterparts in existing systems. We provide a comprehensive query optimizer that automatically selects optimal execution plans based on data characteristics and query specifications. Experimental evaluation on distributed clusters processing massive-scale mobility and social network data demonstrates that GeoGraphStream achieves orders-of-magnitude improvements in discovery quality and processing efficiency compared to specialized systems. This work establishes a new paradigm for distributed data mining that fundamentally changes how complex multi-dimensional data environments are analyzed.

Real-time recommendation in dynamic environments requires systems that continuously adapt to evolving user preferences and item characteristics while maintaining prediction quality under strict latency constraints. Current recommendation systems struggle to balance exploration-exploitation trade-offs in streaming settings, often sacrificing long-term user satisfaction for short-term engagement metrics. This paper presents StreamRec+, an improved recommendation architecture that advances state-of-the-art approaches to contextual bandits-based streaming recommendations. The system introduces a hierarchical context decomposition mechanism that separates stable preference patterns from transient interests, enabling more nuanced adaptation strategies. We design a novel sliding window ensemble that dynamically weights different temporal models based on their recent performance, achieving superior accuracy across diverse recommendation scenarios. The architecture incorporates an efficient cache-aware update mechanism that reduces computational overhead while maintaining model freshness. A key innovation is the multi-armed bandit module with automatically tuned exploration rates that respond to environmental volatility, achieving improved performance across different data stream characteristics. Extensive evaluation on large-scale benchmark datasets demonstrates that StreamRec+ consistently outperforms existing streaming recommendation algorithms across multiple evaluation metrics including prediction accuracy, catalog coverage, and long-term engagement. The system operates within strict latency constraints, making it suitable for production deployment in high-throughput environments.
